# One report for everything: MultiQC {#sec-multiqc}

**Rule:** `multiqc` · **Tool:** MultiQC 1.28 · **Input:** every per-sample
output · **Output:** `QC/{runName}_multiqc_report.html` and
`QC/{runName}_multiqc_data/`

## The problem it solves

By now each sample has a FastQC report per read, two trimming reports, a Salmon
log and a flagstat file. With 12 samples that's dozens of files to open.
**MultiQC** searches a folder for logs from tools it recognises, pulls out the
numbers, and makes **one HTML page** with every sample side by side. Outliers
are much easier to spot this way.

## What bagPipes runs

```bash
module load multiqc/1.28
multiqc -f output/* -o output/QC
mv output/QC/multiqc_report.html output/QC/{runName}_multiqc_report.html
mv output/QC/multiqc_data        output/QC/{runName}_multiqc_data
```

`-f` overwrites an old report. `output/*` means "look through everything in
`output/`". This rule runs last in `RNApipeCore` because its inputs include
every other output. Once it finishes, Snakemake deletes the `temp()` files
(FastQC, trimming reports, trimmed FASTQ;
see [the map](pipeline-map.qmd#the-output-folder)).

## Reading the report, section by section

Open the HTML file in a web browser. The top **General Statistics** table has one
row per file. Then there's one section per tool, in pipeline order:

| Section | Look at | Good sign | Red flag |
|---|---|---|---|
| **General Statistics** | Read counts, % aligned, % duplicates, GC % | Replicates look alike | One sample far off in any column |
| **FastQC** | Per-base quality, adapter content, GC | All lines bunched together | One sample's line separate from the rest |
| **Cutadapt / Trim Galore** | % bp trimmed, filtered reads | Low, similar across samples | One sample losing many reads |
| **Salmon** | Mapping rate, fragment length | Similar across samples; 70–90 % mapped | One sample much lower |
| **Samtools (flagstat)** | Mapped %, properly paired % | > 85–90 % | Big drop in one sample |

The plots are interactive: hover to see sample names, click a sample in the
toolbox to highlight it, and use *Export* to save a figure.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The most useful thing MultiQC tells you

Not absolute numbers, but **which sample doesn't look like the others**. If
one replicate has half the mapping rate, double the adapter content or a
different GC curve, find out why before trusting its counts.
:::

## The data folder

`{runName}_multiqc_data/` holds the same numbers as plain-text tables, e.g.
`multiqc_general_stats.txt`. You can load these into R or Excel to make your
own QC figures or a supplementary table.

```bash
column -t output/QC/*_multiqc_data/multiqc_general_stats.txt | less -S
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. Why does the `multiqc` rule list the trimmed FASTQ files as inputs, even
   though MultiQC doesn't read FASTQ?
2. One sample has a Salmon mapping rate of 40 % while the others are at 85 %.
   Where would you look next?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. So Snakemake waits for trimming (and everything else) to finish before
   running MultiQC, and keeps the temp files until then.
2. Its FastQC (overrepresented sequences, GC content: rRNA or adapter
   dimers?), its trimming report (how much was removed?) and its HISAT2
   alignment rate (if that's also low: contamination or wrong species;
   if it's high: intronic or intergenic reads, gDNA).
:::
:::
